_why: A guard is proven by breaking the thing it guards and watching it go red. This project does that
and writes what the guard said into the commit message - which is real, and one-time. It cannot be
re-executed. A guard proven in one month and quietly hollowed out in the next looks exactly like a
guard that still works: the suite is green either way.
This ledger is those proofs, kept as data. Each plant is the exact text substitution that puts the
defect back, and the suite that must go RED when it is there. tools/guard/replant.py applies one,
requires the named suite to fail, restores the file byte-for-byte and verifies the restore.
TWO RATCHETS, and both may only fall. `owed` is the number of registered suites with no plant at
all - the honest size of what this ledger does not yet cover. `owed_generalisation` counts plants
marked site_only: the defect was put back at exactly the place it was found, and nothing shows the
guard would catch the same defect somewhere else. PlantLedgerTest holds both to their ceilings and
checks every plant still matches its file exactly once, which is cheap; replant.py actually runs

plants.why: The Zone tab's unload named three of seven editors. The four it did not name were an absence, not a decision, and an editor left showing a zone that is no longer open is what the save path then trusts.

The matrix panel is handed the map view's matrix, so the map view has to have loaded first. That dependency used to be two adjacent lines inside a worker thread and is now the order of two list entries, where nothing about it looks load-bearing.
An empty set of zone editors would show a zone to nobody and report success forever.
The five copies of the && chain got one thing right: short-circuiting. An editor that could not save must not be followed by a reload that throws its work away.
The window handed the Zone tab null for both lists and nothing failed until the user asked for a save or a zone switch.
Applying a paint flushes every open editor first and gives up if one refuses. Built with none, the painter would throw at apply time, having already let the user paint.
plants.must_say: flushes them before it writes anything

plants.why: git normalises endings on commit and restores them per checkout, so hashing raw bytes made the stamp and the mutation baseline say a file had been edited when nothing had.
plants.must_say: saved LF and CRLF hashes the same

plants.why: The other half of the same rule. A .class or a .png differing only in 0x0D bytes IS a different file, and a digest that could not say so would be worth less than the one it replaced.

The ledger's whole value is that a plant which no longer matches its file is a REFUSAL rather than a skip. A rotted plant that is quietly passed over turns this ledger into a list of proofs nobody re-runs, which is the exact thing it exists to replace.

Downloading the source as a zip gives a directory with no .git. git wrote to stderr, PowerShell's Stop preference turned that into a terminating error, and build.ps1 died after compiling and before stamping - then test.ps1 blamed the stamp.

The zone save threw away the boolean the NPC form returned, three lines above another refusal it honoured: an NPC pointing at a script the zone does not define showed 'Script not defined' and the zone was written anyway.

File > Save is openEditors.saveAll(FALSE). The whole single-region save sat inside 'modified && dialog', so a flush that asks nothing fell through to 'return true' and reported every tile edit on a loose GR map as saved while writing none of them.

A region opened on its own has no prop textures - File > Open GR Mapfile passes null. setMaterialTextures then threw inside, straight into showProp's catch-all, and the whole prop editor was left permanently inert with only a stack trace on stderr.

plants.why: updateModel decided the prop had no model slot, loaded a null model, and then carried straight on into models.set() with the very index it had just rejected.

The gizmo used to be bound by indexing the prop list a second time through the selection box, while the rest of showProp used the index it was given. Two sources for one identity: when they disagreed the gizmo stood over a different prop than the form displayed, and with no selection at all it was get(-1), thrown and swallowed.
plants.must_say: the very prop the form is holding

plants.why: Three forms place a new record where the user is looking. Placing it at 0,0 instead drops it in a corner of a map the user may not even have on screen - and the guard that was supposed to catch this asserted the size and the script while saying nothing about x and y, because before the seam existed it could not.
plants.must_say: IT LANDED WHERE THE USER IS LOOKING
